name: Fission
summary: Open-source functions on Kubernetes: a pool of warm, generic pods takes your code on the first call, so cold starts stay around 100 ms.
intro: Fission adds four object types to a Kubernetes cluster as custom resources. An Environment is a language runtime image (Node.js, Python, Go and others); a Package holds your code; a Function ties code to an environment; and a Trigger binds an event to a function. There are four kinds of trigger: an HTTP route, a cron timer, a message-queue consumer and a watch on Kubernetes objects. Every one of them ends up as an HTTP request to Fission’s router, which forwards it to a pod running the function.

Where that pod comes from depends on the executor you pick per function. The default, `poolmgr`, keeps a pool of generic pods warm for each environment. On a first call it takes one out of the pool, copies the package in and tells the runtime to load it, which for a small function typically takes well under 100 ms; the pod is reaped after it sits idle. `newdeploy` instead creates a Deployment, Service and CPU-driven autoscaler per function, and can keep a minimum number of pods running so there is no cold start at all. A third type, `container`, runs your own prebuilt image.

Platform9 started Fission in 2016, and engineers at InfraCloud, which sells a supported version, have maintained it in recent years. Its pace has been uneven: v1.21.0 (January 2025) and v1.22.0 (December 2025) came nearly a year apart, then five releases followed in May and June 2026, up to v1.27.0 on June 22, 2026. Commits continue, but most of them in 2026 come from a single maintainer.
strengths: Fast cold starts from the pre-warmed pool: typically under 100 ms for a small function
Plain Kubernetes underneath: functions are pods and its objects are custom resources, so existing monitoring, RBAC and GitOps tools apply
Pick latency or idle cost per function: warm pool, a per-function Deployment with a minimum scale, or your own container image
Message-queue triggers built on KEDA cover Kafka, SQS, Kinesis, Pub/Sub, NATS, RabbitMQ and Redis lists, and scale their consumers to zero
limits: A small, concentrated maintainer base: most 2026 commits come from one person, after an eleven-month gap between releases in 2025
Scale to zero applies to function pods, not to the cluster: you still run the control plane, nodes and the warm pools
Every invocation passes through the router as HTTP, and `newdeploy` scales on CPU rather than on requests or queue depth
Cold start grows with package size, so large dependencies erode the warm pool’s advantage

snippet.title: Deploy a function, then expose it over HTTP and on a schedule
source: # default executor (poolmgr): code is loaded into a warm pod on first call
fission fn create --name hello --env nodejs --code hello.js
# or: a Deployment + autoscaler per function, with one pod always warm
fission fn create --name report --env nodejs --code report.js \

story: Kubernetes was powerful but asked a lot of a newcomer before anything useful ran. Soam Vasani began Fission at Platform9 in late 2016 so that customers could be productive on the first day they installed a cluster. Platform9 announced it on January 24, 2017, together with its managed Kubernetes service, pitching it as Lambda-style functions that run on any Kubernetes cluster.

The alpha supported Node.js and Python, triggered functions from HTTP routes, timers and Kubernetes watches, and already used a pool of warm containers to keep cold starts near 100 ms. Version 1.0 followed in February 2019. Fission was one of several Kubernetes function frameworks of that period; one of its peers, VMware’s Kubeless, has since been archived (its last commits date from December 2021).

Development then slowed: 2024 brought only patch releases of v1.20, and 2025 just two minor releases, eleven months apart. A burst of work in 2026 brought five releases in two months, including a v1.27.0 rewrite that collapsed the executor’s nine controllers into three.

choices.choice: A pool of warm, generic pods
choices.why: Instead of starting a new container per function, Fission keeps runtime pods already running and loads code into one on demand. That is what brings a cold start down to about 100 ms, at the cost of keeping the pool alive.
Each environment is a container with a small web server and a dynamic loader, much like a buildpack. Adding a language means building an environment image, not changing Fission’s Go core.

choices.choice: Built on Kubernetes, not its own scheduler
choices.why: Its authors expected real applications to mix functions with ordinary microservices, and running both on Kubernetes lets one set of monitoring, logging and deployment tools cover everything.

choices.choice: Every trigger becomes an HTTP call
choices.why: Timers, queue consumers and watchers all post to the same router that serves HTTP routes, so there is a single invocation path to scale and debug.
